vignette: The concrete floor sucks the heat from his knees. It is 1982, and the calendar has long since dissolved into a single word they repeat until it loses all meaning: perpetua. Sleep is the first thing they take, then the illusion of dignity. He learns to pace his breathing the way he would later teach his residents during sleep-deprivation protocols. When the questions stop mattering, the silence between strikes becomes the loudest thing in the room. They drag him to a reinforced window to watch men who once consulted him for his sharp mind and steady hands. When they finally release him, he walks into a night he does not remember entering. He leaves his name, his clinic, and half his life in the dark. Years fold into each other like safe houses and forged papers. He completes his psychiatry training in a northern city that never knows his face. The work arrives easily. He understands the architecture of the autonomic nervous system because he has dismantled his own, piece by piece, to survive. He tells himself this knowledge is a bridge. He builds a quiet life. He buys an apartment with three separate locks. He dates briefly, but the intimacy always feels like a proximity alert. Single by habit, or so he tells himself. At sixty-two, he has learned to call his solitude competence. He sits in his office now, back to the interior wall, chair angled toward the door. The digital clock on his desk ticks with a metronome precision that tightens his jaw. He notices the therapist's pen before their voice. He knows the exact cadence of a deflection, and he listens for it in his own thoughts. When the therapist mentions the word memory, his pulse jumps. He smooths his cufflinks, a gesture he has cultivated to look deliberate. He speaks in measured tones, analyzing his own panic with the detached curiosity of a clinician observing a stranger. Hyperarousal, he thinks, naming it as if taxonomy will drain it. Avoidance is a recognized coping strategy. But his hands are cold. His breath hitches when the elevator dings in the hall. He treats patients with practiced grace, prescribing and listening with a steady rhythm. Yet in his own home, he sets out three different sets of keys, checks the deadbolt four times, and leaves the bathroom light on all night. He tells himself it is professional caution. He knows the symptom clusters by heart. He reads his own flashbacks like case studies. He maps the intrusions that arrive unbidden when the late afternoon light hits his desk at exactly 4:15 p.m.-the smell of damp wool, the echo of a boot heel, the sudden, absolute conviction that the ceiling is lowering. He presses his palms flat against the wood. He waits. The room does not change. He exhales. He folds his hands in his lap. The session concludes. He stands, adjusts his coat, and walks to the door. His step is even, his posture straight. Outside, the street is ordinary. He does not look back. He walks to his car, sits in the driver's seat for a full minute with the engine off, listening to the neighborhood breathe. Then he turns the key.
